blocks.title: One Sentence
blocks.text: `Send` is about what survives an await. `'static` is about what you borrowed.
One Blocked Poll Kills A Thread

items: A blocked `poll` occupies its worker thread entirely
No other task on that thread can run, at all
Tokio multi-thread defaults to one worker per core
N blocking calls stall N cores

blocks.title: Symptoms
items: Latency spikes with no CPU explanation
Timers firing late, heartbeats missed
Throughput cliff under load
`std::thread::sleep`, `std::fs`, `reqwest::blocking`
Synchronous DB drivers, contended `Mutex`
Heavy CPU too: parsing 200 MB JSON, image resize
Hashing a password blocks with no syscall in sight
==tokio-console== shows each task's busy and idle time
`--cfg tokio_unstable` unlocks a poll-time histogram
Any poll over **10–100 µs**: split it or move it off

blocks.title: Async File I/O Caveat
items: On Linux, `tokio::fs` is `spawn_blocking` underneath
Each call hops to the blocking pool and back
Batch file work into one `spawn_blocking` closure

blocks.title: Do The Math
blocks.text: `argon2` at ~100 ms per call saturates a 4-core runtime at just 40 requests/s.

slides.page_title: Blocking Inside Async: The Cardinal Sin

items: `tokio-console` shows per-task poll times and stalls
Or `--cfg tokio_unstable` poll-time histogram metrics
Rule: any poll past 10-100 microseconds gets split or moved
Async file I/O is a lie on Linux
`tokio::fs` is `spawn_blocking` under the hood
`argon2` at 100 ms destroys a 4-core runtime at 40 req/s

blocks.title: Why It Is A Sin
blocks.text: You are not borrowing a thread from a pool. You are freezing the only thread that can make progress.

items: An await adds a poll and a possible queue hop
A hot path with no I/O is faster written sync
Compile time: deep nesting makes huge monomorphized types
Builds get slow and stay slow
Stack traces show executor frames, not your logical chain
Async infects its callers all the way up
A sync trait cannot call async code without `block_on`
A crate must pick tokio vs smol vs async-std traits
`AsyncRead` differs between futures-rs and tokio
In libraries stay runtime-agnostic, or feature-gate it

blocks.title: Do Not Go Async
items: A CLI making three HTTP calls
`ureq` plus threads is simpler and faster to write
You finish before the runtime finishes compiling

blocks.title: Pick By Workload
blocks.text: Count sockets, not opinions. Below a few hundred connections, threads are the cheaper answer.

blocks.title: The Whole Handbook, One Line
blocks.text: Futures do nothing until a runtime polls them, they suspend only at awaits, wakers bring them back, and blocking one poll stops everything.

caption.text: Part 2 of RUST ASYNC, DEMYSTIFIED. Your Rust future did nothing when you called it. That is not a bug — it is the entire design. Ten pages on lazy futures, the state machine under async fn, wakers, runtimes, Send bounds, and the one sin that takes production down: blocking a poll.
